newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope re-opens debate on "birth of France".
newsitem.headline: Pope re-opens debate on "birth of France".

text.p: Pope John Paul said on Wednesday that the baptism of a fifth century pagan king whose conversion he celebrated during a controversial visit to France last weekend had marked the birth of the French nation.
In impromptu remarks in Polish that could re-ignite a dispute with secular critics in France, he linked the baptism of Frankish king Clovis to France's 1,500-year history as a nation.

He had avoided doing so at an outdoor mass for 200,000 worshippers in the cathedral city of Reims on Sunday, winning praise from French commentators for skirting a clash over the country's religious and secular traditions.
Addressing pilgrims from his native Poland, the Pope said:

"When in 1980 I visit the Church of France for the first time I asked the following question: "France, what have you done with your baptism after 15 centuries?'. This visit, this pilgrimage, has been a magnificent response."

He said at the end of his remarks: "Dear pilgrims, give thanks with me for this beautiful, marvellous response to the baptism of a nation which is very close to us (in Poland) and which shows great sympathy for us."
Clovis was a central figure in French history before the 1789 Revolution abolished the monarchy. Born in what is now Belgium, he was baptised in Reims around 496.
He ruled from eastern France to the Netherlands and Germany and extended his kingdom in battles against tribes such as the Visigoths to cover most of modern France.

French secularists had accused the Pope of violating a 1905 law separating church and state by holding the mass in Reims to mark the anniversary of the Clovis baptism, which the extreme-right National Front portrays as France's "birthday".
Protest marches against the visit in Paris and other cities, however, were low key.

The Pope upset France's other religious groups on his first visit in 1980 when he spoke of France's 1,500-year history as a nation. "France, eldest daughter of the Church, what have you done with the promises of your baptism?" he asked then.
He did not refer to France as "eldest daughter of the Church" neither during his latest visit nor at Wednesday's audience.
